title: More Choice, Less Choice: The Paradox of Consumer Autonomy in Algorithmic Markets
content: Digital markets give consumers access to more alternatives than they can realistically examine. Search rankings and recommendation systems help manage this abundance, but they also influence which alternatives receive attention. This paper examines the difference between available and considered choice and its implications for consumer autonomy. We propose a four-stage framework covering available (A), visible (V), experienced (E), and final choice (C), and examine its observable stages using three behavioral datasets: Coveo, RecGaze, and FINN.no. In Coveo, an average of 5.88% of returned search results received a recorded click. In RecGaze, participants visually attended to an average of 39.96 out of 150 available films. FINN.no shows that clicks were concentrated near the top of ranked lists, with stronger concentration in search results than in recommendations. These findings show that the number of alternatives presented to consumers differs considerably from the number receiving recorded attention or interaction. They do not establish that algorithms reduce consumer autonomy. Limited consideration may also reflect consumer preferences and efficient search. We argue that autonomy cannot be assessed from the number of available alternatives alone. For sustainable consumption, this raises a further question: whether environmentally preferable alternatives have a realistic opportunity to enter consumer consideration.
